about: The texts that a server of this release gives an agent, as the agent receives them, each with its SHA-256: the instructions, every tool's title, description and argument descriptions, every guide and recipe, every prompt, and the answers to the first calls on a new org. pnpm agent-texts writes it from what a throwaway server serves, and a test fails while it is stale, so a change to any of these texts shows in this file's diff. The words of other outcomes, of refusals and of failed runs are worded from what each call is given and answers, and the tests of the package that words them pin them.

tiers.1: Always received: the instructions, and in tools/list the title, the description and the argument descriptions of every tool.
tiers.2: The onboarding path, what an agent reads from its first call to its first saved definition: the answers to the first calls on a new org, and the guides and prompts start, first-playbook, give-tools and get-started.
tiers.3: Every other text listed here: the other guides, recipes and prompts.

placeholders: {origin} stands for the server's own address. Where a text is received, {org} and {playbook} stand for the ids in the address, and a required argument of a prompt in braces for the words the person gives. The instructions are as the page at /debug shows them: on a real connection they hold one more sentence, just before the last, which names the caller and the org.

lines: This organization has no playbooks yet. A playbook keeps work your team can use again. Its workflows coordinate functions that reason, interact, predict and compute. Unless the person has already said what they want, ask what they want done, and offer three starts: set up a first playbook, connect a service they use, or hear what Auto can do for their team. Before you build, read the guide start with get_guide: it says which function type each part of a job takes. In Studio, your team can review playbooks and run results. You can also manage workflows, connections, members and billing there. {origin}/studio/?server=%7Borigin%7D&src=agent

Before you build or change anything, read the guide start with get_guide: it says which function type each part of a job takes. Build from the job: each part is a function of the type its work needs, and a workflow runs the parts in order. A playbook holds work that keeps running after a conversation, in any line of business. Auto Runtime makes and runs playbooks; Studio manages them; the agent is a separate client. A playbook contains one brain (its reusable functions) and workflows; runs belong to the playbook. The org is the caller's own: list_playbooks shows its playbooks and create_playbook makes one. A tool that cannot do what was asked says why and what to change.
Create playbook

Creates a playbook for one business responsibility, and returns it empty. Use it when the person wants something done that should keep working after this conversation, and none of their playbooks covers it. Each job it does again and again is a workflow, and each part of a job a function of the type that part needs. An id that is taken or retired is refused. `playbook` is the id every tool inside it takes, and `description` what it is for, in the person's words.
The id of the playbook: 3 to 48 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter
The display name of the playbook: 1 to 100 characters, not all whitespace
What the playbook is for: up to 2000 characters, or empty
List playbooks

Use it when the person speaks of their playbooks, or wants something done that one of them may cover. Lists the playbooks of the org that the caller may access, sorted by id. Each holds every field of the playbook, such as its name, what it is for and whether it is active.
Whether to list retired playbooks as well; false when left out
Get playbook

Reads one playbook by its id, active or retired, with the source of its page. Use it to read the playbook's page, or a playbook whose id is known; list_playbooks finds the others. `playbook` is its id.
Update playbook

Changes the name, the description or the page of an active playbook and returns it. Use it when the person renames a playbook, changes what it is for or gives it a dashboard. What is left out stays as saved.
Its page as YAML, data and runs, as the page guide says; null removes it
Retire playbook

Retires a playbook and returns it: it stays readable with its history, takes no changes or runs, and keeps its id, so no other playbook takes it. restore_playbook brings it back. Use retire_playbook when the person asks to retire that playbook; update_playbook changes its name or description. Retiring a retired playbook changes nothing.
Restore playbook

Restores a retired playbook and returns it, active again under its own id, with its functions, workflows, page and history as they were when it was retired. Use it when the person asks to bring back a retired playbook; list_playbooks with include_retired lists the retired ones. Restoring a playbook that is not retired changes nothing.
List comments

Lists the comments people made in Studio, newest first, the open ones unless `open` is false: with `playbook`, that playbook's, and without it, the organization's own, on its connections, members, Settings or itself. Use it when the person says they left comments in Studio or pastes the line Studio copies; the organization's own and each playbook's are listed apart. Each names what it is about by its `address`, which says which tool reads and changes the thing, such as get_definition for a step or list_connections for a connection. `address` keeps the comments on one thing, and with `under` those on everything under it, such as the events of a run. Once one is acted on, resolve_comment closes it, with the same `playbook` or none; its `studio` is its place in Studio to give the person.
The id of the playbook to act in; left out, the organization's own
An address of a thing of the playbook, or of the organization for its own comments: keep the comments on it
true keeps the comments on address and on every address under it, such as the events of a run; it may then name a definition without its version
true keeps the open comments, false the resolved ones; true when left out
How many comments a page holds, 1 to 200; 50 when left out
The next_cursor of the page before
Resolve a comment

Resolves a comment people made in Studio, so it leaves the open comments and the activity: with `playbook`, one of that playbook's, and without it, one of the organization's own. Use it once what the comment asked is done, with `how` acted, or with `how` dismissed when the person says to drop it. `id` is the id of the comment, as list_comments gives it, with the `playbook` it was listed with, or none. Resolving a comment resolved already records nothing and answers it as it stands.
The id of the comment, as list_comments gives it
acted once what the comment asked is done, or dismissed to close it without acting
List models

Lists the models this server can call, by the id a reasoning function gives as its model, written provider/model. An id ending in * stands for any model of its provider and is not one to run. Use it before a reasoning function names its model, or when a run says its model is not offered.
Lists only the models this provider prefix serves, such as anthropic or the name of a gateway
Search tools

Searches the tools of the tool servers this playbook's functions may use, named in a function's tools as server/tool or server/* and called by query_connection or execute_connection. It lists the servers, and every tool while they offer at most 100, or with `terms` the tools that match, best first, each marked reads if it only reads, acts if it may change something, or unmarked, counted as acts. A server that cannot be asked says why. Each server names the playbooks it serves. With `terms` naming a service, `providers` lists those a person may connect that no server serves yet.
The id of a playbook, to search only the tool servers its functions may use; without it, every tool server of the org
Words to find tools by, up to 8 of up to 64 characters, separated by spaces; a word counts most in a tool's name, then in its arguments, then in its description
Searches only the tool server of this name, as a function writes it before the slash
read keeps the tools marked reads, write the others
List the tools of a connection

Lists the tools a connection's server offers now, those its entry allows, by name, a page at a time. Each has its title where the server gives one, its whole description, its hints and its mark. Use it to show the person what one connection can do; search finds tools across servers. `cursor` is the next_cursor of the page before.
The id of the connection
The most items to answer with, from 1 to 100; 20 when left out
The next_cursor of the page before, or the cursor of an item, to read on after it
Add connection

Starts connecting a person's account at a service, by the name of a provider that search lists, or a server given by hand as name, type, entry and credential. Once approved, the connection's tools serve the org's playbooks. Work out first what the runs will do at the service and what must exist there, and ask for the access both take; the guide connect-a-service says how. With more, a group the provider offers beyond its first consent, the page asks its scopes too. An MCP server given by hand says how it authenticates: leave its credential out unless the answer says it names none, and a secret takes instructions and key_page. It answers pending with a link to Studio's page, where the person approves it within 24 hours. Nothing is granted by this call and no credential passes through it.
The name a function gives the server, in lowercase and hyphens
A provider to connect, by its name
With provider, its placeholders' values
mcp for a remote MCP server, given url; openapi for an HTTP API, given document
The tool server, without its credential
The https URL of the MCP server
The https URL of the OpenAPI document of the HTTP API
The https URL the API's calls go to, in place of its document's
Headers sent with each request, never a secret or a reference
Query parameters sent with each call, never a secret or a reference
The tools a function may name; every tool when left out
The playbooks that may use it, by id; every one when left out
Whether calls are kept whole in the playbook's history; true when left out
The header or result metadata key of the server's id of a call

How the server is credentialled, never its value, which the person gives on the page; leave it out for an MCP server given by hand, which says how it authenticates, and name a kind only for one that names none
For reference, the variable of the runtime that holds the value, such as CRM_API_KEY
For secret and reference, the header, query parameter or security scheme the value is sent as
For secret and reference, what name is: header, or for an HTTP API query, a query parameter, or security, a security scheme of its document
For a header, the scheme written before the value, such as Bearer
For client_credentials, the https URL of the authorization server
For client_credentials, the id of the client, else given on the page
For client_credentials, the scopes, separated by spaces, none when left out
For a provider's authorization, own for the organization's own OAuth client, its client ID and secret given on the page; the default where the way takes no client here

For secret, Markdown without HTML the page shows the person: where the key is made, with a link, the plan or role and permissions it needs, and its format, as: Make a key under [Settings, API keys](https://acme.example/keys) as an Admin, with read access. It starts with `acme_`.
For secret, the https page where the person makes the key
For secret, the key with … in place of its characters, such as acme_…
For secret, the regular expression from ^ to $ the key matches, such as ^acme_\w+$; a key that misses it is kept

A group of more the provider's way offers, by name, as search lists under providers; its scopes are asked on the page beside the first consent's. None when left out, and an addition by hand takes none
List connections

Lists the connections of the org, newest first. Each has its server, whether it is pending, connected or broken, and the groups of more it may still be granted. Use it to see which tool servers people added, and whether the person approved one add_connection added.
Whether to list removed connections as well; false when left out
Reconnect connection

Issues a new link to Studio's page for a connection that is broken, or whose link ran out, so the person gives its credential or signs in again; the link before stops working, and nothing else changes. Use it where list_connections or search says a connection is broken and its reason says to reconnect it. With more, a group list_connections offers, the link asks its scopes beside those the connection holds. It answers the connection with the link, which the person who added it opens within 24 hours, or, where a broken connection sends a variable of the runtime that is set, connected again at once.
A group list_connections offers the connection, by name; a plain link when left out
Remove connection

Removes a connection of the org for good: no playbook may use it any more, and its credential is forgotten. Use it when the person asks to remove that connection. Removing a removed connection changes nothing.
Activate license

Activates the license of this runtime with the key Studio gave as the account holder or an organization admin registered it, alk.<org>.<runtime id>.<secret>. The license covers the whole runtime, every org of it: from then on it starts runs on the credits of the org at Auto, without asking Auto for each, and reports the runs it started every hour, and sooner once it has used half of what its license left it. It answers where the runtime stands, as get_license does, and keeps the key in its secret store so it stands after a restart. A key Auto does not know, one that was replaced or one for another runtime is refused as a conflict of the kind license_invalid, and a key of a closed org as account_closed.
The key Studio gave as the account holder or an organization admin registered this runtime, alk.<org>.<runtime id>.<secret>
List generation models

Lists the models a generation function may name, from this server's catalogue, with what each produces and takes, and the gateways a function names a model through. A function names its model as gateway/model, such as auto/openai/gpt-image-2. A retired model is listed so a saved function that names it can be explained; it is not one to name. Use it before a generation function names its model or its parameters.
Lists only the models that produce this kind: image, audio or video
Create definition

Saves a new function or workflow from its document, without running it. update_definition changes one saved, and a name is never reused. Each part of a job is its own function, of the `type` its work needs, and `name` is how workflows and tools refer to it. A workflow owns one job the business does again and again, and a check, a test or a setup is not one. `source` is the whole document in its type's format, which get_guide gives, and `overview`, optional, Markdown for the person who runs the business. A function needs `diagram`; a workflow takes none. The document's `page` shows the person its runs; write it as the page guide says. A document that does not fit its format is refused with the line and what is wrong.
The id of the playbook to act in

By each part's job: reasoning only interprets, judges or writes; lookup reads a service or earlier runs; interaction asks a person or has a service act; prediction forecasts a quantity; computation calculates or transforms exactly; generation makes images or audio; workflow runs the parts in order.
The definition name: 3 to 48 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter
The definition document in its type's format, at most 65536 bytes in UTF-8

Write a plain-language Markdown overview: what this definition does, why it is needed, and how it fits the playbook. Use only supplied context, in one to three short paragraphs, with no diagram. Avoid invented benefits.

Required for a function, refused for a workflow: Mermaid source of a flowchart or a state diagram of how the function works, its first line flowchart, graph or stateDiagram, or the word none when a picture would add nothing
List definitions

Lists the definitions of one type in the playbook, sorted by name, each with its version, its status and what its document says it does, without the document. Use it to find a function or workflow the person names, or to see which exist before one is made; get_definition reads one with its document. `type` is the type to list, and `include_retired` adds the retired definitions.
The definition's type
Whether to list retired definitions as well; false when left out
Get definition

Reads one definition with its document, active, paused or retired, with its version and the input and output its document declares. For a workflow it also returns its triggers, the event trigger and the schedules that start it on its own. A definition whose document has a page answers page.runs and how its views stand; `render: true` previews the page. Use it to show the person a definition or to learn the input a run takes; list_definitions lists the definitions of a type. `type` is the definition's type and `name` its name.
True to render its page now
With render, an output to render result over, as of a run that succeeded
Update definition

Replaces the document of an active definition and returns its new version, used from then on. Use it when the person changes a saved definition; a retired one cannot change. `type` and `name` say which, `source` is the whole new document, and `overview` Markdown for the person who runs the business, written again each time; left out, the saved one stays. A function needs `diagram` each time; a workflow takes none. A document that does not fit its format is refused with the line and what is wrong; one the same as saved, with the same diagram and its overview the same or left out, records nothing.
Pause definition

Pauses a function or workflow and returns it: while it is paused, neither its triggers, nor run_definition, nor a workflow's step starts a run of it, and the runs already going finish. The times and events its triggers meet while it is paused are never run, and resume_definition lets it run again. `type` and `name` say which definition and `reason` says why; pausing one already paused changes nothing.
Why the definition is paused, kept with it while it stays paused, 1 to 1024 characters
Resume definition

Resumes a paused function or workflow and returns it, so that it can be run again. Its triggers start runs from the first time or event after it is resumed, and nothing they met while it was paused is run. `type` and `name` say which definition; resuming one that is not paused changes nothing.
Retire definition

Retires a function or workflow, with its page, and returns it: it can still be read and listed, but it neither runs nor changes, and no other definition takes its name. restore_definition brings it back, paused. Use retire_definition when the person asks to retire that definition; update_definition changes one. `type` and `name` say which definition, and retiring one already retired changes nothing.
Restore definition

Restores a retired function or workflow, with its page, and returns it: it comes back paused, under its own name and with its history, and starts no runs until resume_definition resumes it. A playbook restores a definition within the bounds it creates one under. `type` and `name` say which definition; restoring one that is not retired changes nothing.
Run definition

Runs a function or workflow with an input and records the run. A run that ends within its call answers its result; one that finishes later answers started with a run_id unless it ends before its first wait; get_run shows how it ended. A workflow does a job the person wants done again; a function runs alone to be tested, and in workflow steps. `type` and `name` say which definition, `input` is the value it takes, as the input_schema get_definition shows, and `run_id` is optional: the same id retries safely, since a run that ended or waits answers as it stands and one that failed runs again. A function that calls a tool may change something outside the playbook, so a run of one that did not succeed is never run again under its id; list_playbook_events with its run_id shows what it called.
The run input: any JSON value the definition takes, {} when left out, at most 262144 bytes as JSON in UTF-8 and 512 levels deep
The run's id, a UUID in any case, kept in lowercase
Get run

Reads one run of the playbook by its id: the definition and version that ran, who started it and when, its status, and its output or why it did not succeed, with the record its type keeps, such as the tokens of a reasoning function or the tool a lookup function called. A run is started until it ends as succeeded, rejected or failed. Use it to tell the person how a run ended; list_playbook_events with its run_id shows each step and tool call of the run. A run whose definition has a page answers page.result. `run_id` is the id run_definition answered with or was given.
Cancel run

Cancels a run that is still going, such as a workflow or a reasoning function, at the request of the person: the request is recorded on the run at once, and the run ends as cancelled within a moment, a reasoning function's before its next call, a workflow's steps stopped and the runs they wait for cancelled too. It cannot be undone, and what the run did before it ended stays done. Use it when the person asks to stop that run; a run that ends within its call, as a computation function does, a prediction function asked a question or an interaction function that calls a tool, cannot be cancelled. `run_id` is the run's id and `reason`, kept on the run, says why; asking again records nothing more, and get_run shows how it ended.
Why the run is cancelled, in words the run's history keeps, 1 to 1024 characters
List runs

Lists the runs of the playbook a page at a time, newest first, each with its definition, its status, who started it and when it ended, without its output. Use it to find a run the person means, such as the runs of a scheduled workflow; get_run reads one run in full. `type` and `name` keep the runs of one definition and `status` those in one status. A filtered page looks at up to 1000 runs, so it may hold fewer runs than `limit`, or none, while has_more is true. `cursor` is the next_cursor of the page before.
Only the runs of this type
Only the runs of the definition with this name
Only runs in this status: started, succeeded, rejected or failed
false leaves out the runs a workflow's step started; true when left out
List playbook events

Lists what happened in the playbook a page at a time, newest first: definitions saved and retired, runs started and how they ended, the steps of workflow runs, tool calls, and the events published to it, each with a summary in plain words, its fact as data with a large field as its size, and its metadata; get_event reads one event whole. Use it to follow the playbook's activity, to see what one run did, or to find the events a page or a workflow's schedule can take. `type` keeps one type of event, `run_id` one run and every run it started, `since` what was recorded from that time on, and `cursor` is the next_cursor of the page before. The playbook's own creation, update and retirement are not among the events; list_playbooks shows them.
The next_cursor of the page before, to read on after it
A time in ISO 8601; only what was recorded from then on
Only the events of this type, by its public name
The id of a run that no other run started: only what it and the runs it started recorded
asc for oldest first, desc for newest first
Get event

Reads one event of the playbook whole by its id, as list_playbook_events shows it: its fact as data and its metadata, every field whole, with a tool call's arguments, the tool's result as it answered and the answer document read from it. Over MCP an input, output, record, answer, arguments, result or event data past 65536 bytes appears as its size; over HTTP every field is whole. Use it to open what a tool answered, or a large input or output, that a page of events shows as its size. `event_id` is the event's id: a UUID, or for a workflow's step its record's id, an underscore and its number.
The event's id: a UUID, or a step's record id followed by an underscore and the step's number
Publish event

Publishes an event to the playbook, where a workflow whose schedule names its type starts a run and a page that filters on it folds it into its views, and returns its id and time. Use it when something outside the playbook happened that the playbook should react to or remember; send_run_event gives an event to one waiting run. `event` is a CloudEvents event with a `source` and a `type`, and publishing the same source and id again records nothing, so a call can be retried with its id. The playbook's own types and sources, such as those of its runs and definitions, and the lineage attributes it gives its own records, are refused.
A CloudEvents 1.0 event of at most 245760 bytes as JSON; any other attribute is an extension, its name 1 to 20 lowercase letters and digits, its value text, a boolean or an integer
The version of CloudEvents the event follows; 1.0 when left out
The id of the event, unique among the events of its source; made when left out, 1 to 256 characters
Where the event comes from, a URI reference such as /ledger/eu, 1 to 1024 characters
What happened, such as com.acme.ledger.month-closed, 1 to 256 characters
What the event is about, within its source, 1 to 1024 characters
The media type of data, such as application/json, 1 to 256 characters
The schema data follows, an absolute URI, 1 to 1024 characters
What the event carries, any JSON value that nests at most 510 levels deep
When it happened, in RFC 3339, such as 2026-10-05T09:00:00Z; when the playbook records it, if left out
Introspect a tool

Describes one tool of a tool server this playbook's functions may use, whole: what it does, the JSON Schema of the arguments it takes, its server's hints and its mark. Use it once search has found a tool, before writing its arguments or naming it in the tools of a function as server/tool. Its server is asked for its tools when this is called, and nothing is sent to the tool; dry_run checks arguments, and query_connection or execute_connection calls it. `server` and `tool` name the tool as search lists it.
The tool server, as search names it and a function writes it before the slash
The tool of that server, as search lists it and a function writes it after the slash
Dry run a tool call

Answers what execute_connection would check for one tool and its arguments, without calling the tool: whether the caller may call it, whether the playbook is retired, whether whoever runs this server allows the tool, its mark, whether the arguments match its input schema and whether its server can be reached just now. Use it before execute_connection when a call may act, or when the arguments are unsure. Nothing is sent to the tool and nothing is recorded. `server` and `tool` name the tool as search lists it, and `arguments`, when given, are the object to check.
The arguments of the call, an object in the shape of the tool's input_schema, at most 256 KiB as JSON
Query a connection tool

Calls one tool marked reads of a connected service this playbook's functions may use, on the service's own API as its tool list names the tool, with the arguments it is given, and answers what a run of a function would see. Use it to read what a tool answers, or to find an id a function needs; it refuses a tool not marked reads, which execute_connection calls. The call is live and acts as the playbook, so it needs the permission to change the playbook; search with only read lists the tools it calls. It is recorded in the playbook's history, with its content where the server's entry keeps it. `server` and `tool` name the tool as search lists it, and `arguments` is the object its input_schema takes.
Execute a connection tool

Calls one tool of a connected service this playbook's functions may use, whatever its mark, on the service's own API as its tool list names the tool, with the arguments it is given, and answers what a run of a function would see. Use it when the person asks for what a tool that may change something does, such as sending, creating or deleting, and to set a service up for the playbook, before its runs act on it. The call is live and acts as the playbook, so it needs the permission to change the playbook; search says the mark of each tool, and dry_run what this would check. It is recorded in the playbook's history, with its content where the server's entry keeps it. `server` and `tool` name the tool as search lists it, and `arguments` is the object its input_schema takes.
Answer a request

Answers a request a function's run waits on; the run takes the answer within the host's sweep, a second by default, and an interaction function's run succeeds with it. Use it when the person approves, rejects, revises or otherwise answers a request list_interactions shows, held for an agent or sent through a tool; a new run asks again and answers nothing, and send_run_event gives an event to a waiting workflow. `run_id` is the run of the request, and `answer` takes the shape of the request's answer_schema, which list_interactions shows, such as {"decision": "approve"}. `claimed_for` is whom the caller says it answers for, kept as a claim. The same answer again answers as before, another is a conflict, and one that does not match leaves the request open.
The answer, a JSON value the answer schema of the request takes
Whom the caller says it answers for, kept with the answer as a claim and never checked, at most 256 bytes
List open requests

Lists the open requests of the playbook, newest first: what each function asked, of whom, through which tool or held for an agent, until when and how its delivery stands, with the `run_id` that answer_interaction takes. Each carries its `answer_schema`, the shape answer_interaction checks an answer against, as recorded when asked, which get_definition may no longer show; null for a notification. Use it when the person asks what the playbook is waiting on, or to find the request they answer. `to` keeps the requests to one party, `type` to one type of function and `function` to one name, which with `type` names one function; `cursor` is the next_cursor of the page before. Every reader of the playbook sees each party and message, as a run’s input is seen.
Only the requests to this party
Only the requests of functions of this type
Only the requests of functions of this name, of the type given if any
Get asset

Reads one asset of the playbook by its id: its media type, size and SHA-256, the model that made it, if any, when it was kept and when it expires or expired, and whether its content was removed. It answers an `address` its bytes are read at without a key, signed as it is read, until `address_until` 15 minutes later; both are null once the asset expired or where the runtime signs none. Use it to show an asset after the address in its run's output expired, or an image a tool answered. `id` is the asset's id, as either gives it.
The asset's id, a UUID in any case, kept in lowercase
Send event to workflow run

Gives an event to one workflow run that is still going, for a step that listens for it, such as an approval, and returns the event with its id. Use it when the person answers what a run waits for; it does not start a run, and publish_event gives an event to the playbook as a whole. `run_id` is the workflow run's id and `event` has a `type` and an optional `source`, `subject`, `data` and `id`; an event whose id the run already received is ignored, so a call can be retried with its id. An event no step takes yet waits in the run. The playbook's own types and sources, and the lineage attributes it gives its own records, are refused.
The id of the workflow run, a UUID in any case, kept in lowercase
An event for a workflow to listen to, after the CloudEvents attributes, at most 262144 bytes as JSON in UTF-8
What happened, such as com.acme.approval.decided, at most 256 characters
What the event is about, at most 1024 characters
The payload of the event, any JSON value that nests at most 510 levels deep
An id of the event; an event is delivered to a workflow once per id. Made when left out, at most 256 characters
Get guide

Reads one of the playbook's guides. Use it before building: the guide start says which function type each part of a job takes, and which guide each task needs. A format guide says how to write that type of definition, with its examples and bounds, and a recipe how its task is done. `guide` names one of them, and the answer is its whole text in Markdown. It holds the recipes first-playbook, connect-a-service, give-tools, schedule and keep, which the tools listed here can follow.

# Create your first playbook

A first playbook starts from the job the person wants done again and again. Break the job into its parts, give each part a function of the type its work needs, and write the workflow that runs the parts in order. Read a type's guide with get_guide before you write a function of that type, and the workflow guide before you write the workflow. Every function and workflow you write carries its `page`, which shows the person what each run achieved and what the runs add up to. Read the page guide with get_guide, and write each page in its document as the page guide says. When you create or run something, the response includes `studio`, a link to its page in Studio. Give that link to the person. A reasoning function needs a model the runtime can call. Hosted Auto supplies models. On a self-hosted runtime, the operator configures a model provider: https://on.auto/docs/self-host/configuration#models.

1. Call list_playbooks, and list_models where this connection has it to see the models this server can call. When it lists none and says in `provider_setup` how the person adds a model provider, help them do that first.

2. Ask the person what the playbook is for, in their own words, and the first job it should do again and again: what it is given or must find, what it must work out, who must decide or be told, and the result they want from it. Then learn how its work starts: on its own at set times, on its own whenever something arrives, or only when someone asks. Where their words already say so, such as "every morning", "continuously" or "whenever one arrives", take that as the answer and say so rather than asking again. When more than one model is offered, ask which to use; a model whose id ends in `*` stands for many and is not a model to run. Where a person must approve or decide, ask once where they want to be asked. It can be through a connection that sends them a request and reads their reply, such as a chat, an email provider or a ticketing app, or through you (`deliver: agent`). A request saved with neither is refused, and the refusal names the connections that can send it and read the reply. Ask once, too, where a notice goes: a channel or their direct messages.
3. Say the job back to the person as its parts, in the order they happen, and give each part its type by what the part does, not by how it is done:
- it interprets, judges or writes: a reasoning function
- it reads what a connected service holds, or what earlier runs of the playbook produced: a lookup function
- it asks a person and takes their answer, or has a service act: an interaction function
- it forecasts a quantity from the playbook's own history: a prediction function
- it calculates or transforms data exactly: a computation function
- it makes an image or audio: a generation function

The order of the parts, the branches, the waits and what happens when a part fails belong to the workflow, never to a prompt. Four shapes show the range. A job that only judges what the person gives is one reasoning function. A job that only calculates is one computation function. A job that reads, calculates and writes is a lookup function, a computation function and a reasoning function. A job that reads, judges, asks and then acts is a lookup function, a reasoning function and two interaction functions. Agree the parts and their types with the person before you write anything.
4. Create the playbook with create_playbook, with the person's words on what it is for, or use the playbook they name when list_playbooks shows it.

5. Write each function in the format of its type's guide, in the order the job uses them, each with its `page` in the same document. A reasoning function takes the facts it judges as its input, which the workflow hands it. For a part that reads from a service or acts on one, follow the give-tools recipe. It makes a read a lookup function and an act an interaction function. A reasoning function names tools in `tools` only where its model must choose among them. Where that service is not connected yet, connect it with the connect-a-service recipe. Or build without it for now, so that the person sees a run today. Let the workflow take what a part would read as its input, pasted by the person. Ask a person through you (`deliver: agent`). Leave a part that has a service act, or sends a notice, until its service is connected, and tell the person it is not built yet. Show the person the documents and ask whether to save them.

6. Once they agree, save each with create_definition, with its `type`. A function needs `diagram`: Mermaid source of how it works, or the word none. A workflow takes none. `overview` is optional: Markdown that tells the person what it does and why it is needed. A name that is taken is refused. Choose another with the person rather than change the function that has it.

7. Test each function that can run now with run_definition on a made-up input, and tell the person what it answered, in their words. These need no connection: a reasoning function, a computation function and an interaction function held for you (`deliver: agent`). A test of an interaction function held for you (`deliver: agent`) waits for its answer. list_interactions shows the request, and answer_interaction answers it once the person says what to answer. A function that has a service act really acts when it runs. Run it only once the person agrees. A prediction function answers once the playbook has history.

8. Read the workflow guide with get_guide and write the workflow that owns the job, whose steps call the functions in order and hand each one what the steps before it answered: one step is enough when that step finishes the job, and a later ask changes the workflow. Write its `page` in the same document: the outcome of each run as a headline with its key figures, and the main number of each period. Where the work starts on its own, give it a `schedule`, as the triggers guide says. A `schedule` holds its triggers: `cron` or `every` for set times, and `on` for what arrives. For set times, use `cron` with `time_zone` naming the person's time zone, or `every`. A run on a clock is given its due time alone. So its first steps are the lookup functions that find its material, or the workflow gives it a fixed input in `input.from`. For what arrives, use `on` with a filter on an event `type` named in the past tense, such as `com.example.item.received`. A run is then given a list holding the event, and the workflow passes the event's `data` to its first step. Where the material comes from sources not yet connected, start with `on`, so that the person starts runs today with material they paste, and move to a clock once lookup functions reach the sources.
9. Show the person the workflow's document, and save it with create_definition, `type` workflow, once they agree.

10. Run the workflow once, in one of two ways, never both. Where it starts `on` an event, publish the material they paste with publish_event, as an event of that type with a `source` that names where it came from and an `id` of its own, such as `test-1`. A real event's `source` and `id` would make that event a repeat, ignored when it comes. The event starts the run, so a moment later find it with list_runs, `type` workflow, and read it with get_run. Otherwise, start the run with run_definition. A step held for you (`deliver: agent`) waits for its answer, which you give with answer_interaction, as in a test. Tell the person what the run answered, in their words. Where the workflow starts on its own, tell them too when it next runs, in their own time, or what starts it.

Then tell the person what they can do next: change when it runs with the schedule recipe and the triggers guide, or connect the services its parts still wait for, with the connect-a-service and give-tools recipes. Once it has more than one workflow, give the playbook a page with update_playbook, led by each workflow's main number.
Connect a service

Connects a service the team uses to Auto, asking for the access the playbook needs to run and to be set up there, in one approval where the provider offers it, sets the service up once the person agrees, and says what it can do.
The service to connect, such as Slack or Google Drive
Connect {service} to Auto for my team, then tell me what it can do.
# Connect a service

A playbook's runs act on the services connected to the org, and expect what they act on to be there already: a team with the statuses work moves between, a channel, a label, a folder, a project. A run does not set a service up, nor does it check that one is set up. You do, here, with the person, before the first run, and you ask for the access that takes when you ask for the connection.

1. Before you connect anything, work out two things with the person: what the playbook's functions and workflows will do at the service, run by run, and what must exist there first for that to work. Name each thing, and whether it is there already.

2. Call search with `terms` for both kinds of work: the tools the playbook's functions will call, and the tools that create what must exist. Where the person named a server, give its name as `server`. Call introspect for the input_schema of a tool before writing its arguments.

3. When no server offers them, and search answers `providers`, call add_connection with the name of the provider that serves what the person wants, and in the same call ask for what setting the service up needs: where search lists a group of `more` under the provider that covers it, name it in `more`, so the person approves once. Where none of the provider's tools can make what must exist, and the service has an HTTP API or an MCP server that can, add that too, by hand: for an MCP server, `authorization` first, the credential's `kind` alone, and where the runtime answers that the server offers no consent or that it cannot connect it by consent, how it takes its key, never the key. Give the person each link add_connection answers, on which they approve it, signing in or giving the key. Where search answers no `providers`, tell the person that whoever runs this server sets tool servers up in its settings file, `auto-runtime.yaml`, under `tool_servers`; the server reads them when it starts again, and nothing more can be done here until then.

4. When a server says it cannot be asked just now, tell the person why, in its words; whoever runs the server can look into it. Where search says a server's connection is `connection_broken` and its words say to reconnect it, call reconnect_connection with its `connection` as `id` and give the person the link it answers, rather than removing the connection and adding it again. Where the service is connected already and lacks the access setting it up takes, list_connections offers the groups the connection may still be granted; ask for one with reconnect_connection, given its name as `more`, and give the person that link.
5. Once list_connections says a connection is connected, read what the service holds with query_connection, and tell the person what you found and what you would reuse.

6. Show the person what you would create and change. Once they agree, make each change with execute_connection and read it back with query_connection. Where no connected tool can make a change, tell the person exactly what to change in the service and where, and read it back once they say it is done. Never make a function or workflow to set a service up or to check that it is set up: that is your work, with these tools, before the first run and whenever something there changes.

7. Keep the ids you read, such as the team's and each status's, for the functions that use them. Then tell the person what is set up and what the connection can do, and give the playbook its tools with the give-tools recipe.
Give the playbook tools
Puts the tools of a connected service to work: a lookup function for a read, an interaction function for an act or a question, and a reasoning function's tools only where its model must choose.
The tool server whose tools to give, as search names it
Give the playbook tools.
# Give the playbook tools

A tool of a connected service is put to work by the function type its use needs, and the tool itself says which: search gives each tool a `mark`. A read the job always makes, by a tool marked reads, is a lookup function: one call and no model. An act, by a tool marked acts or unmarked, is an interaction function, which calls it with `call`: it answers at once and spends no model call. A reasoning function names tools in `tools` only where its model must choose among them while it runs, because which to call, or how often, depends on what they answer. Read a type's guide with get_guide before you write a function of that type. Every function and workflow you write carries its `page`, which shows the person what each run achieved and what the runs add up to. Read the page guide with get_guide, and write each page in its document as the page guide says. A reasoning function needs a model the runtime can call. Hosted Auto supplies models. On a self-hosted runtime, the operator configures a model provider: https://on.auto/docs/self-host/configuration#models.

1. Call search to see the tool servers this playbook may use and their tools, each with its `mark`; when the person named a server, give its name as `server`, and give `terms`, a few words of what the person wants done, to find the tools that fit among many. Call introspect for the input_schema of a tool before writing its arguments.

2. When no server is listed, or not the one the person wants, or search says a server's connection is `connection_broken`, follow the connect-a-service recipe: it connects the service, or reconnects it, and sets it up for what the playbook will do there; then call search again. When a server says it cannot be asked just now, tell the person why, in its words; whoever runs the server can look into it.

3. To learn what a tool answers, call it yourself with the arguments its input_schema takes and read its `text`: that is what a run of a function will get. Never save a function only to see what a tool answers. Call a tool whose `mark` is reads with query_connection. A tool whose `mark` is acts or unmarked may change something, so call it with execute_connection, and only once the person agrees. When a function needs an id, such as a channel's, call the tool that lists them and take the id from its answer, confirming the choice with the person.
4. Ask the person what the playbook should do with the tools, and give each use its function:

- a read the job always makes, by a tool marked reads: a lookup function, whose `call` names the `server` and the `tool`, with its arguments in `with`, written from the run's input. One lookup function for each read.
- an act on a system, or a read by a tool that is not marked reads: an interaction function that calls the tool with `call`, written from the answer execute_connection gave.

- a question to a person: an interaction function too. Ask once where they want to be asked, then name in `deliver` the connection's tool that sends the request and in `replies` the one that reads the replies, or write `deliver: agent`.

- a choice among tools that the model must make while it runs: a reasoning function whose `tools` name only those tools. Hand it as input what lookup functions already read, so that it calls a tool only for what it could not be handed.
5. Write each function in the format of its type's guide, with its `page` in the same document, show it to the person, and save it with create_definition, with its `type`, once they agree.

6. Run each with run_definition. A function that has a service act really acts when it runs, so run it only once the person agrees. A run that called tools and did not succeed is not run again under its id, since a tool may have changed something: read what it called with list_playbook_events, given its `run_id`, and start a new run only if the person still wants one.
7. Tell the person what each run did with the tools, and that a function can call only the tools it names.

8. Then, with the workflow guide, write or change the workflow that owns the job the person wants done again, whose steps are the functions, with its `page` in the same document: the steps that read come first, and each later step is handed what the steps before it answered. Save it once they agree, run it, and tell the person what it answered and what they can do next.

# Run a workflow on a schedule

A workflow can start on its own: at set times, in UTC or in a time zone it names, every so often, or whenever an event of a given type is published to the playbook. Read the workflow guide and the triggers guide with get_guide before you write one.

1. Ask the person which workflow to run and when, such as every weekday at 9:00 their time, or whenever the month's books are closed. Find the workflow with list_definitions, `type` workflow, or write one in the format of the workflow guide. Its document carries its `page`, so the person sees what each run did while they were away: keep it, or write it in the same document, as the page guide says.

2. Give the workflow a `schedule` as the triggers guide says, with one trigger or up to three, each kept on its own: `cron` with five fields, minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, read in UTC or in the time zone `time_zone` names beside it; `every` with a duration of at least a minute; and `on` with the type of the events that start it. A run its schedule starts runs as the playbook itself, with its due time, or a list of the event, as its input, and its history says which trigger started it.

3. When the times are the person's own, such as 9:00 their time, put `time_zone` beside `cron` with the IANA name of their time zone, such as `America/New_York` or `Europe/London`, and write the five fields in their time: the runs then stay at their hour when the clocks change for daylight saving. Leave it out only for times meant in UTC. `every` takes no time zone.

4. A run on a clock is given its due time alone, so it finds what is new from that: what came since the time before, such as in the 30 minutes before `schedule.due` for `every: PT30M`. A time skipped while the run before still ran, or one whose run failed, is not run again, so give the workflow an input of its own too, such as `since` and `until`, with which the person runs it by hand for a stretch it missed, and let `input.from` take either: `'${ $data.schedule === undefined ? $data : ({ since: new Date(Date.parse($data.schedule.due) - 1800000).toISOString(), until: $data.schedule.due }) }'`. In a time zone, the stretch between two daily times is 23 or 25 hours on the nights the clocks change.

5. To start a workflow when a step of another one ends, give it `on` with a filter on that step's run: `type: run_succeeded`, a `subject` naming the function, such as `computation/work-out-order`, and `calldepth: 1`, which a run by hand does not carry. Or have the other workflow `emit` an event of a type of your own; in a `for`, it emits one for each item.
6. Show the person the document, and save it with update_definition, or with create_definition for a new workflow, once they agree.

7. Tell the person when it runs next, in their own time, and that every run is kept in the playbook's history. Auto does not list the times ahead, so work the next one out from the trigger. `every` counts from the save that gave the trigger its present form, the workflow's `created_at` where it has not changed since; a later save that leaves it as it is keeps its times.
8. To see how its runs went, call list_runs with `type` workflow and the workflow's `name`, and get_run for one run, whose headline says what it did.

9. A run an event started that was rejected or failed is not started again, and the same event published again is a repeat, which records nothing. list_runs with `status` rejected, or failed, finds such runs, and list_playbook_events given a run's `run_id` shows its input, the list holding the event. To finish its work, run the workflow by hand with the event's `data`, which `input.from` takes as it takes the event: `'${ Array.isArray($data) ? $data[0].data : $data }'`.
# Workflow format

A workflow coordinates a playbook's functions through steps. The API stores it as a definition of the type `workflow`. Its source document is YAML in the [Open Workflow Specification](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification) DSL 1.0, within the rules and limits on this page. [Build your first workflow](https://on.auto/docs/tutorials/first-workflow) is a guided example, and [Workflows and runs](https://on.auto/docs/concepts/workflows) explains how a run starts, waits and ends.

A workflow does none of the work itself: each step that reads, calculates, judges, asks or acts calls a function of that type. The order, the branches, the waits and what happens when a step fails are the workflow's, never a prompt's. A workflow of one step is the job when that step is all the job does; a workflow made only to see a function answer is a wrapper, not a job.
## A workflow document

This workflow reviews a campaign brief, then asks the brief's owner to approve the review. It calls two functions: the reasoning function `review-campaign-brief`, whose document follows it, and the interaction function `approve-campaign-brief`.
