### A run that ended a moment ago

A question counts every run that ended before it started. Before it reads the dataset, it waits until the dataset has folded what the playbook had recorded when the question started. That takes moments: the time it takes to fold a page of events, as the views of pages are kept, and up to a pass (a second) for an event another server recorded. A dataset that has not caught up within 3 seconds is read as far as it has folded, and the record's `dataset_checkpoint` says how far that was. So a question asked in the step after a run, in the same workflow, counts that run, and needs no wait or retry before it.

Whether the run falls in the window depends on its period. The window ends at the origin, the period before the one the question is asked in. A run read with `time: event` falls in the period it ran in, which no question reads until that period has passed. A run about a period that has ended, such as last week, carries a date of that period in its output for `time` to read; Forecast from a run the workflow just recorded shows one.
A run that has not ended when the question starts, such as one another workflow records at the same time, is not counted. Ask once it has ended.
### The lines on a page

A chart draws each line of a series under its name. A page that draws a prediction as it is shows `observed` and `predicted`, or `observed` and `total`, in the chart's legend. To show them in the person's words, rename them where the page reads the prediction. In a page's `result`, the `replace` filter renames them in the JSON the chart reads, as the page of the example does: it leads with the likely orders of the next week, and draws the weeks observed as `Orders` and the weeks ahead as `Forecast`.

Over the answer above, its headline is `About 140 orders in 2026-W42 (128 to 151).` A template prints a number as it is. A forecast's figures are often not whole, since a range's ends are interpolated between misses, so the headline rounds each with `round`. `round: 1` keeps one decimal: `4.800000000000001` prints as `4.8`.

A workflow whose output carries the prediction under a field, such as `forecast`, renames `output.forecast` the same way. A page's fold that keeps predictions in a view for `runs` names each line as it builds it; see Its page.
## How a run ends
A question ends within its call and cannot be cancelled while it runs:
| Ending | When |
| `succeeded` | The prediction is its output |
| `invalid_input` | The input is not a question the function takes, or the series is not in the dataset's window, at `/input/series` |
| `conflict`, kind `history_too_short` | The series' history is too short for the forecaster to backtest an answer; the detail names the periods it has and the period from which it answers |
| `unavailable`, kind `dataset_not_ready` | The dataset is waiting or rebuilding; with `because` `stalled`, it stalled |
| `failed` | The runtime itself broke down |
## Bounds
A save is refused past these bounds:
| Bound | Value |
| Horizons | 1 to 8, each 1 to 52 periods |
| History | 0 to 500 periods, at most the window |
| A total | A day to a week, a month or a quarter, at most 7, 31 or 92 days; a week to a quarter or a year, at most 14 or 53 weeks; a month to a quarter or a year, at most 3 or 12 months |
| Window | At least the longest horizon and 3 more periods, or for a total 4 times the most periods its enclosing period holds, which the forecaster needs to backtest; at most 1,000 |
| Season | 2 to 366 periods |
| Coverage | 0.5 to 0.95, 0.8 when left out |
| Filters | 1 to 8 |
| Functions a playbook | 32 active or paused, unless the server's `PREDICTION_MAX_FUNCTIONS` says otherwise, from 1 to 1,000. Retiring one frees its place |
The data and the runs are bounded so:
| Bound | Value | When it is reached |
| A series | 1 to 256 bytes of text | The event is passed over |
| A question's run | 10 seconds, within its call | A workflow's call waits for it that long and a minute more |
| A question's wait to read | 3 seconds | The question reads the dataset as far as it has folded then |
## In a workflow

A workflow calls a prediction function as it calls any function, with `call: run_definition` and `type: prediction`. The task's output is the run's output; see [Calling a function](https://on.auto/docs/reference/workflow-format#calling-a-function).

- A question, such as `{ call: run_definition, with: { type: prediction, name: weekly-orders, input: { series: north, horizon: 1 } } }`, ends within its call, written out or computed at run time. Its own maximum is 10 seconds, so the task waits at most 10 seconds plus one minute.

This workflow forecasts a region's orders for next week from `weekly-orders`. The task's output is the series the function answers, and a workflow that needs one number reads the likely value of the first predicted point, `lines[1].points[0].value`. While the region's history is too short to forecast from, the workflow returns no forecast:
```yaml
document:
namespace: orders
name: next-week-orders
version: '1.0.0'
summary: Forecasts a region's orders for next week, or returns none while its history is too short.
input:
schema:
document:
type: object
properties:
region: { type: string }
required: [region]
do:
- forecast:
try:
- ask:
call: run_definition
with:
type: prediction
name: weekly-orders
input:
series: '${ $data.region }'
horizon: 1
output:
as: '${ ({ forecast: $data.lines[1].points[0].value }) }'
catch:
errors:
with: { status: 409 }
when: '${ $error.kind == "history_too_short" }'
do:
- none: { set: { forecast: null } }

`run_definition` of `next-week-orders` takes an input such as `{"region": "north"}`. Once the region's history holds enough weeks, the run succeeds with `{"forecast": <the likely value>}`, such as `{"forecast": 140}`. Before that, its question is refused `conflict` with the kind `history_too_short`; the `catch` takes it, and the run succeeds with `{"forecast": null}`. To keep the range too, read the whole point, `lines[1].points[0]`, which holds its `at`, `value`, `low` and `high`. Any other refusal ends the workflow's run, as below.
A run that does not succeed raises the error of its rejection:
- A refusal raises status 503 for `unavailable` and 409 for `conflict`, with its `kind` and `because`.
- A dataset still being built passes with time, so a retry on status 503 suits a question.

- A `stalled` dataset does not change when tried again, nor does `history_too_short` before the period its detail names. So leave 409 out of a retry policy, and read `$error.because` in a `when` to leave out a stalled dataset.
### Forecast from a run the workflow just recorded

A workflow that records a period and then forecasts from it asks in the step after the record, as A run that ended a moment ago says. This prediction function, `weekly-revenue`, reads the weeks that the computation function `record-week` recorded. `record-week` returns what it is given, `{ store, week_start, revenue }`, where `week_start` is the Monday of the week, such as `2026-10-26`:
```markdown
description: Predicts the revenue of each store next week, from the weeks record-week recorded
predicts:
target: revenue
period: week
horizons: [1]
unit: USD
data:
events:
- type: run_succeeded
subject: computation/record-week
time: /output/week_start
series: /output/store
target: { of: /output/revenue, as: last }
window: 104
This workflow records the week just ended, then forecasts the next one:
```yaml
document:
namespace: finance
name: close-and-forecast
version: '1.0.0'
summary: Records a store's revenue for the week just ended, then forecasts next week's from it.
input:
schema:
document:
type: object
properties:
store: { type: string }
week_start: { type: string, format: date }
revenue: { type: number }
required: [store, week_start, revenue]
do:
- record:
call: run_definition
with:
type: computation
name: record-week
input: '${ $data }'
- forecast:
call: run_definition
with:
type: prediction
name: weekly-revenue
input:
series: '${ $data.store }'
horizon: 1
- `record` runs `record-week`. Its run's end is the record `weekly-revenue` reads, and its output, what it recorded, is the data of the next step.
- `forecast` asks for the next week. Its origin is the week before the one the workflow runs in: the week just ended, which the question counts, as `record` ended before it started.

Run on Monday 2 November 2026 with `{"store": "north", "week_start": "2026-10-26", "revenue": 48210}`, the run succeeds with the prediction, whose last observed point is `{ "at": "2026-W44", "value": 48210 }`. An older week, as a backfill records, falls in the window too, and the forecast counts it in its own week.
## The overview

`create_definition` and `update_definition` take an `overview` beside the document: Markdown for the person who runs the business, written from everything known of them and of the playbook. It says why the function exists, what it does and how it fits, in one to three short paragraphs; less technical, more value. Write it after the document, and write it again with every update.

They also take a `diagram`, every time, so that whether the function is drawn is a choice its author makes: Mermaid source of a flowchart or a state diagram of how the function works, whose first line is `flowchart`, `graph` or `stateDiagram`, or the word `none` when a picture would add nothing. A save without it is refused. A diagram holds at most 8,192 bytes in UTF-8, and Auto Studio draws it under the overview. It is read there at full size in a column, so draw it top to bottom, as `flowchart TD` or a state diagram, in three to eight nodes, each a few plain words for the person who runs the business rather than an expression or code.

An overview holds 1 character to 16,384 bytes in UTF-8. The version keeps it as written, and `get_definition` returns it so until an update gives another; an update that leaves it out keeps the overview saved. `list_definitions` leaves it out. [Reasoning functions](https://on.auto/docs/reference/http#reasoning-functions) gives the rules every definition follows, with `used_by`, the definitions of the playbook that use this one.
## Its page
A prediction function's page is the `page` key of its front matter, written with the document and saved with it. It shows the person what is coming, and how well the forecasts held:

- `result`: the forecast as a line, with its horizon: a headline with the likely value of the period ahead and its range, and a chart of the periods observed and those ahead, as The lines on a page shows. An answer does not name its series, and `result` reads no input. To name the series in the headline, the workflow that asks can give the series' name as the label of a mark, such as `marks: [{ label: 'North, last week', value: 136 }]`. The answer carries the mark back, so `result` reads the name as `output.marks[0].label`, and the chart draws the mark as a level. An answer to a question asked without marks has none. Read the label through `default`, as `{{ output.marks[0].label | default: "This series" }}`, since a missing field stops the render.

- `runs`: the forecast against what happened. A fold keeps, for each period, the value forecast for it and, once the period has passed, the value a later answer observed, as two lines of one series. An answer does not name its series, so keep this view for a function asked of one series, or read the series from the output of the workflow that asks. `weekly-orders` is asked of each region, so its page has no `runs`, which would mix the regions.

Show numbers over time as a chart keyed by the period a run is about, and anything else in its clearest form: a table, a list or a sentence. Show the value of the work, not telemetry: never how long the runtime took, a model's tokens or a run's id. [Page format](https://on.auto/docs/reference/page-format) says how to write `data`, `result` and `runs`.
## Availability

Prediction functions are available in every runtime. The runtime keeps the datasets and forecasts in its own process, with nothing to install. See [Functions and availability](https://on.auto/docs/concepts/functions#availability).
# Computation function format

A computation function is a definition of the type `computation`. Its document declares the input and output contracts, and holds a TypeScript program that computes the output from the input. A run calls the program's function with its input, and the value the function returns is the run's output.

Use one for the arithmetic and data shaping a language model should not do: totals, paces, projections and transformations of rows of figures. It reaches nothing outside the playbook and asks no model: reading a service is a lookup function's work, and judging or writing a reasoning function's.
What a run returns depends only on its input and on the moment the run started:
- The program sees nothing but its input. It has no network, no files, no environment and no randomness.
- `Date.now()` and `new Date()` return the moment the run started, which stays the same for the whole run.
- So the same input and the same start time give the same output, on the same build of the runtime.
- A program that never reads the clock gives the same output for the same input on every run. A program that reads it may give a different output on a new run, since each run has its own start time.

Numbers are double-precision floating point. Integers are exact only up to 2^53. There is no decimal type, and nothing rounds to decimal places. So compute money in whole minor units, such as cents, as the example below does. See Numbers.

export default function (input: Input): Output {
const { days_elapsed, days_total } = input.period;
if (days_elapsed > days_total) {
throw new Error(`days_elapsed ${days_elapsed} is past days_total ${days_total}`);
const campaigns = [...Map.groupBy(input.rows, (row) => row.campaign)]
.toSorted(([first], [second]) => (first < second ? -1 : 1))
.map(([campaign, rows]) => {
const budget_cents = rows[0].budget_cents;
const spend_cents = rows.reduce((sum, row) => {
if (row.budget_cents !== budget_cents) {
throw new Error(`The rows of ${campaign} disagree on its budget: ${budget_cents} and ${row.budget_cents}`);
return sum + row.cost_cents;
const projected_cents = Math.floor((spend_cents * days_total) / days_elapsed);
const pace_permille = budget_cents === 0 ? null : Math.floor((projected_cents * 1000) / budget_cents);
return { campaign, spend_cents, budget_cents, projected_cents, pace_permille };
return { campaigns, total_spend_cents: campaigns.reduce((sum, each) => sum + each.spend_cents, 0) };
`Input` and `Output` are the input and output schemas as TypeScript types, which the runtime declares for the program; see Types.
The schema and the program keep the arithmetic exact and the rows consistent:

- The schema bounds the input: at most 4,000 rows, each cost from 0 to 5,000,000 cents, each budget from 0 to 1,000,000,000 cents, and periods of 1 to 366 days. An input outside those bounds is `invalid_input`, with a pointer to each value.

- With those bounds, the largest intermediate value, `projected_cents * 1000`, is at most 4,000 × 5,000,000 × 366 × 1,000 = 7.32 × 10^15. That is below 2^53, so every value stays an exact integer; see Numbers.

- The program checks what a schema cannot say. Rows of one campaign must carry the same budget, and `days_elapsed` may not pass `days_total`. Otherwise it raises an error, and the run ends as a `conflict` of the kind `unworkable`, such as `The program raised an error on line 63: Error: The rows of spring-sale disagree on its budget: 800000 and 750000`.
- A budget of 0 gives a `pace_permille` of `null`.

To save it, call `create_definition` with `type: "computation"`, the `name` `campaign-pace`, which its page's filter names, the document as `source`, and its `overview` and `diagram`. A save without a `diagram` is refused, so give the word `none` when a picture would add nothing; The overview says how to write both. To run it, call `run_definition` with the same type and name, and with `rows` and `period` in the `input` object. Both operations also take the playbook id, unless the MCP connection is scoped to that playbook.

## Fields
| Field | Required | Value |
| `description` | No | Text of 1 to 1,000 characters |
| `language` | Yes | `typescript`, the playbook's one language |
| `input.schema` | No | A JSON Schema of the input. The input may be any JSON value it allows |
| `output.schema` | No | A JSON Schema of the output. An output that does not match it ends the run as a conflict |

| `output.shape` | No | The name of an [output shape](https://on.auto/docs/reference/output-shapes), `series`, `categories`, `table` or `text`, whose schema is the output schema. Not allowed beside `output.schema` |
| `page` | No | The [page](https://on.auto/docs/reference/page-format) that presents its runs |
- Unknown fields are rejected. Among them are the fields of a reasoning function that do not apply here: `model`, `config`, `tools`, `output.format` and `input.default`.
- The body after the front matter is the program. A document without one is rejected.
- The saved function has the `media_type` `text/markdown`. Its `description`, `input_schema` and `output_schema` come from the document.

- Quote a text that holds ` #`, or a comma inside `{ }`, such as `description: 'Posts the notes in #deliveries'` or `{ note: 'Costs 1,000 a month' }`. Unquoted, YAML reads ` #` as the start of a comment and a comma there, even the one in `1,000`, as the start of another key, so the text ends early, and the save does not always say so.
## The program
The program is one TypeScript module whose default export is a function `(input: Input): Output`.
- It reads its input as its argument, and its return value is the run's output.
- It may declare types of its own and exported functions, and nothing else at the top level, so that two runs share nothing. Write a helper inside the function that uses it, or export it.
- It sees nothing else: no network, no files, no environment, no randomness and no time zone. The clock it reads is the moment the run started.
### Types

The schemas the document carries are the types the program is checked against. `Input` is `input.schema` and `Output` is `output.schema`, as TypeScript types. A document without a schema gets `Json`, any JSON value, for it.
| Schema | Type |
| An object schema with `properties` | A closed type of those properties, the `required` ones required, unless `additionalProperties` opens it |
| An object schema without `properties` | An object of any JSON values |
| `enum` and `const` | A union of their values |
| `anyOf` and `oneOf` | A union of their types |
| An array | Its `items` as the type of its elements, however many `maxItems` allows |
| A definition under `$defs` or `definitions` | A type of its own, named after its schema and the definition, so a `$ref` may refer to itself |

A definition's type is named such as `Input_address` for `#/$defs/address` of the input schema. A character a name cannot hold is written as its code point between two `$`, as `Input_street$45$address` for `street-address`.

What a type cannot say, such as `minimum`, `maximum`, `multipleOf` and `format`, is checked when the run checks its input and output. A `format` is one of `date`, `date-time`, `time`, `email`, `uri` and `uuid`, as [Answers that are JSON](https://on.auto/docs/reference/reasoning-format#answers-that-are-json) sets out, so an input of April for a `date` is refused before the run, with the words `expected a date such as 2026-04-01`. A `pattern`, and any other `format`, are refused when the document is saved. Where a text must take another form, say so in the function's overview.
### Checked when it is saved

The document is checked when it is saved, with the TypeScript compiler, in the strict mode with `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`. It is checked against `Input`, `Output` and the sandbox's own library, so a name the sandbox lacks is a name the compiler lacks. Each problem is refused with its line and the compiler's words:
| Written | Refused with |
| A syntax error | The compiler's diagnostic at its line |
| A type error against `Input` or `Output` | The compiler's diagnostic, such as `Property 'perod' does not exist on type 'Input'. Did you mean 'period'?` |
| An `enum`, a `namespace` or a parameter property | `This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled.` |

| An `import`, `require`, `eval`, `new Function`, `import()`, `import.meta` or a declared name such as `declare global` | `A program reads nothing but its arguments: it imports no module and builds no code` |

| A top-level statement other than a type or an exported function, such as `let`, a class or a function the module does not export | `A module holds its types and its exported functions and nothing else, so that two calls share nothing` |
| No default export, or one whose type is not `(input: Input) => Output` | `The program is a module whose default export is a function (input: Input): Output`, and the compiler's words |
| `async`, `await` or a generator exported | `The program is a function that answers at once; it awaits nothing` |

| More than 500 assignments to variables in one function, counting `+=`, `++` and the like, reported at the 501st | `A function may assign to its variables at most 500 times, since the compiler's analysis of each assignment grows with the others; keep the values in a list, an object or a loop` |

| A name the sandbox lacks: `fetch`, `setTimeout`, `console`, `process`, `Intl`, `Math.random`, `WeakRef`, `Promise`, a local-time method of `Date`; also `new Date(2026, 0, 1)` and `Date()`, which read the time zone | The compiler's words, such as `Cannot find name 'fetch'.`, `Property 'random' does not exist on type 'Math'.` or `Cannot use namespace 'Intl' as a value.` |
| `language` other than `typescript` | `The playbook's one language is TypeScript; write the program as a TypeScript function` |
A program that passes the check can still raise an error when it runs, such as `throw new Error("no rows")` or reading a field of `null`; see How a run ends.
How long the check may take:
- The check runs on a worker of its own beside the runs. The server starts that worker for its first check, which waits up to 10 seconds for it, and then keeps the worker however long it idles.
- Its cost is the compiler's, and depends on the server and on how much the types make the compiler work.

- A save allows the check 2 seconds of the server's wall-clock time, counted from a ready checker. A check that does not finish within them leaves the document unsaved, as `invalid_input`: simplify its types or split the program.
- A busy server may also have slowed the check, so a document near the bound may pass when it is saved again later.
- A save that finds no checker ready is `unavailable`; save it again.
### The sandbox

The program runs in QuickJS compiled to WebAssembly. The runtime pins the build `@jitl/quickjs-wasmfile-release-sync` 0.32.0. That build counts the work a program costs, so this page notes any new build.

The library is the language's own, ES2023 and more, such as `Array.prototype.toSorted`, `Map.groupBy`, `Object.groupBy`, `Set.prototype.union`, the iterator helpers and `BigInt`. What would read the host is gone or fixed:
- `Date.now()` and `new Date()` return the moment the run started.
- These dates work: `new Date(number)`, `new Date(date)`, a date alone such as `new Date("2026-01-01")`, and a date and time that names its offset, such as `new Date("2026-01-01T09:00:00Z")`.

- These raise a `TypeError`, since they read the server's time zone: `new Date(2026, 0, 1)`, a date and time without its offset, calling `Date` without `new`, `String(date)`, a template literal of a date, and `toLocaleString()`. Use `Date.UTC(...)`, the `getUTC…` and `setUTC…` methods and `toISOString()`.

- These are absent: `Math.random`, `eval`, `Function`, `WeakRef`, `FinalizationRegistry`, `Promise` and every local-time method of `Date`, and also `console`, `fetch`, timers, `Intl` and modules. A program returns at once, and the sandbox never runs a `Promise`'s callbacks. A `Promise` would only let a program silently do nothing, so the check refuses one at save.
- Strings compare and sort by UTF-16 code unit: `sort()` without a comparator sorts by code unit, and `localeCompare` reads no locale.
- The output keeps the order its keys were written in. A program that wants sorted keys sorts them.
The output is the returned value as JSON. These values cannot be JSON:
- a `Date`, a `Map`, a `Set`, a class instance or a typed array;
- a boxed number, text or boolean;
- a function, a `BigInt` or a symbol;
- `NaN`, `Infinity` and `undefined`;
- an empty place in an array, and a cycle.
Returning one ends the run as a conflict that names where the first was found, such as `The answer holds a Date at $.campaigns[0].at, which JSON cannot carry`.
### Numbers
Every number is an IEEE 754 double:
- Integers are exact up to 2^53, 9,007,199,254,740,992: `9007199254740992 + 1` is `9007199254740992`. A total or an intermediate product past it, such as `spend_cents * days_total`, loses precision.
- Decimal fractions are approximations: `0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3` is `0.6000000000000001`, and `Math.round(1.005 * 100)` is `100`.

- There is no decimal type and no rounding to decimal places. Keep amounts in whole minor units, such as cents. Multiply before you divide, and end a division with `Math.floor`, `Math.ceil` or `Math.round`, as the example's `projected_cents` and `pace_permille` do.
- `NaN` and `Infinity` are not JSON values, so a run whose output holds one ends as a conflict.
- `BigInt` computes exactly but cannot be an output; turn it into a number or a string first.
- The functions that approximate, such as `Math.pow` and `Math.log`, give the same result on every run of one build of the runtime. Their last digits may differ between builds.
## How a run ends

A run checks the input against `input.schema`, then calls the program. It checks that the returned value is JSON, then checks it against `output.schema`, or against the shape `output.shape` names with the rules the shape adds, such as the order of a series' points. It ends in one of these ways:
| Ending | When |
| `succeeded` | The program returned a value that is JSON and matches the output schema |
| `invalid_input` | The input does not match the input schema, with a sentence and a pointer for each problem, or nests deeper than 512 levels |
| `conflict`, kind `unworkable` | The program raised an error, including a stack overflow |
| `conflict`, kind `unworkable` | The program did more work or used more memory than a run may |
| `conflict`, kind `unworkable` | The program returned what JSON cannot carry, or a value deeper than 512 levels |
| `conflict`, kind `unworkable` | The program returned what the output schema refuses, or what does not fit the run's record |
| `unavailable` | The run took longer than a run may, or found no turn to run within its time |
| `failed` | The runtime itself broke down |
A `conflict` of the kind `unworkable` says what went wrong:
- It names the program's own error and the line of the document it came from, such as `The program raised an error on line 21: Error: no rows`.
- Or it names the bound the program reached, such as `The program did more work than a run may, 20000 checkpoints, and was stopped`.
- The text of the program's error is cut at 1,024 bytes of UTF-8 and marked with `…`. So are the pointer and the detail of each issue of an output the schema refuses, each on its own.
- Running it again with the same input gives the same result, unless the program reads the clock. So a retry does not help: update the definition, or change the input.
- `get_run` shows the kind on the run's rejection, and `list_runs` shows it in the listing.

A run that succeeds records `language`, `work` (the checkpoints it spent) and `duration_ms`. It also records `input_bytes` and `output_bytes`, the sizes of its input and output as JSON. `get_run` returns that record with the output.
## Bounds
| Bound | Value | When it is reached |
| Document | 65,536 bytes in UTF-8, as every definition | Refused when saved |

| The check at save | 2 seconds of the server's wall-clock time on the check's own worker, counted once it is ready. That worker starts at the server's first check, which waits up to 10 seconds for it, and the server keeps it | The save is `invalid_input`: simplify the types or split the program, or save it again when the server is less busy; with no checker ready, `unavailable` |

| Assignments | 500 to variables in one function, counted before the compiler analyses them. Its analysis grows with their square: 500 cost it 43 ms, and 1,000 cost 249 ms | Refused when saved, `invalid_input` |
| Input | 256 KiB as JSON, as every run, nested at most 512 levels | `invalid_input` |
| Work | 20,000 checkpoints, counted as below the table | `conflict`, `unworkable` |
| Memory | 256 MiB, the maximum of the run's sandbox | `conflict`, `unworkable` |

| Stack | 1 MiB, which a function that calls itself reaches after 5,459 calls. The overflow is an error the program may catch, at the same depth every time | `conflict`, `unworkable` when the program does not catch it |
| Depth of a value | 512 levels, in the input and in the output | `invalid_input`; `conflict`, `unworkable` |
| Regular expression | Bounded by the work and the duration: the engine interrupts a pattern that backtracks | As work |
| Output | 1,048,320 bytes as JSON: 1 MiB less 256 bytes kept for the run's record | `conflict`, `unworkable` |
| Text of an error | 1,024 bytes of the program's error, then `…`. The same cut applies to the pointer and to the detail of each issue of an output the schema refuses | Cut, in the `conflict` |
| Duration | 10 seconds from the start of the run, its wait for a turn included | `unavailable` |
| Runs at once | 4 by default, which the operator can change with `COMPUTATION_WORKERS`, and one check at a time beside them; a run waits for its turn within its 10 seconds | `unavailable` |
A run's output and its record share 1 MiB, as for every run; see [Runs and results](https://on.auto/docs/reference/http#runs-and-results).

Work is counted in checkpoints of the engine, so it does not depend on the machine. The engine counts one checkpoint every 10,000 of its steps, where a call or the jump of a loop is a step. A checkpoint is about 0.037 ms of a loop that does nothing on the machine measured below. The same program and input spend the same checkpoints on every run and every host of the same build.

- The example above spends no checkpoint on 1,000 or 2,000 rows, and 1 checkpoint on 3,911 or 4,000 rows. The largest input a run takes holds 3,911 such rows (262,092 bytes). So the bound on work stops a program whose work grows faster than its data, never the example.

- A checkpoint counts the engine's steps and not its native work, such as one `JSON.stringify` of a large value. That is why the duration bound stands beside it. A loop whose body is one native operation over a large value, such as `JSON.stringify` or `join`, spends few checkpoints. Such a run ends at its 10 seconds.
Measured on Node 26.10.0 on an Apple M4 Max:
- The example over 3,911 rows took 5.1 ms in a fresh sandbox.

- One checkpoint of a loop that does nothing took 0.037 ms: a run's 20,000 took 0.74 s. So the 20,000 checkpoints of a run take from under a second to about eleven seconds of interpretation, depending on what each step does.

- A run took about a millisecond more than its program, with or without an output schema, in a worker the server keeps ready between runs. A worker's first run pays its start, about 106 ms. So does the first run after a minute without runs, about 137 ms.
- A run that never returned was stopped 1.5 ms after a deadline of 500 ms.
## In a workflow

A workflow calls a computation function as it calls a reasoning function, with `call: run_definition` and `type: computation`. The task's output is the function's output; see [Calling a function](https://on.auto/docs/reference/workflow-format#calling-a-function).
- The function reaches nothing outside the playbook, so a workflow may run it again freely: its result does not depend on how often it ran.
- A run rejected with `conflict` raises a `runtime` error with status 409. The error's `kind` is `unworkable`, whether the program raised, did too much work or used too much memory.

- A retry gives the same result for the same input, unless the program reads the clock, so a retry policy should not match status 409. Retry on status 503, which a run that was `unavailable` raises, as the example below does.
This workflow reads a month's campaign costs through a tool server, computes the pace of each campaign and has a reasoning function write a summary:

- The first function is a [lookup function](https://on.auto/docs/reference/lookup-format), since its tool is marked `reads`. It returns the rows the tool gives, checked against its output schema, with no model to read them.

- A run of it that called the tool and did not succeed is never run again under its run id. A retry starts a new run, which reads again; see [Retrying under a run id](https://on.auto/docs/reference/http#retrying-under-a-run-id). A lookup changes nothing, so a retry on status 503 is safe.
- The arithmetic happens in the computation function, and the words in the reasoning function.
The lookup function `read-campaign-costs`:
```markdown
description: Reads the cost rows of every campaign for a month
call:
server: ads
tool: campaign-costs
with:
month: '{{ input.month }}'
read: /rows
input:
schema:
type: object
properties:
month: { type: string }
required: [month]
output:
schema:
type: array
items:
type: object
properties:
campaign: { type: string }
cost_cents: { type: integer }
budget_cents: { type: integer }
required: [campaign, cost_cents, budget_cents]
The computation function `campaign-pace` is the document at the top of this page. The reasoning function `write-pace-summary`:
```markdown
description: Summarizes the pace of each campaign for its owners
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5
input:
schema:
type: object
properties:
campaigns: { type: array }
total_spend_cents: { type: integer }
required: [campaigns, total_spend_cents]
Write three sentences for the campaign owners about this month so far. A pace of 1000 per mille means a campaign is on course to spend exactly its budget. Use the figures as given; they are in cents.
Campaigns: {{ input.campaigns | json }}
Total spend in cents: {{ input.total_spend_cents }}
The workflow `campaign-pace-report`:
```yaml
document:
namespace: campaign-reporting
name: campaign-pace-report
version: '1.0.0'
summary: Reads a month's campaign costs, computes each campaign's pace and writes a summary.
input:
schema:
document:
type: object
properties:
month: { type: string }
period: { type: object }
required: [month, period]
do:
- read:
call: run_definition
with:
type: lookup
name: read-campaign-costs
input: { month: '${ $data.month }' }
output:
as: '${ ({ rows: $data, period: $input.period }) }'
- compute:
try:
- pace:
call: run_definition
with:
type: computation
name: campaign-pace
input: '${ $data }'
catch:
errors:
with: { status: 503 }

delay: { seconds: 2 }
limit:
attempt: { count: 2 }
do:
- give-up:
raise:

type: https://example.com/errors/pace-unavailable

- write:

`run_definition` of `campaign-pace-report` takes an input such as `{"month": "2026-09", "period": {"days_elapsed": 12, "days_total": 30}}`. The run reads the rows, computes them, and ends with the summary as its output.

When the computation function's run is `unavailable`, the `compute` task retries it up to twice, 2 seconds apart. Then `give-up` raises an error that names what failed, and the run ends `rejected` as `unavailable`; [Errors, retries and timeouts](https://on.auto/docs/reference/workflow-format#errors-retries-and-timeouts) explains this pattern. When the program raises an error or reaches a bound of its sandbox, the run ends `rejected` at once, and its history shows the computation function's run with its line and error.
## The overview

`create_definition` and `update_definition` take an `overview` beside the document: Markdown for the person who runs the business, written from everything known of them and of the playbook. It says why the function exists, what it does and how it fits, in one to three short paragraphs; less technical, more value. Write it after the document, and write it again with every update.

They also take a `diagram`, every time, so that whether the function is drawn is a choice its author makes: Mermaid source of a flowchart or a state diagram of how the function works, whose first line is `flowchart`, `graph` or `stateDiagram`, or the word `none` when a picture would add nothing. A save without it is refused. A diagram holds at most 8,192 bytes in UTF-8, and Auto Studio draws it under the overview. It is read there at full size in a column, so draw it top to bottom, as `flowchart TD` or a state diagram, in three to eight nodes, each a few plain words for the person who runs the business rather than an expression or code.

An overview holds 1 character to 16,384 bytes in UTF-8. The version keeps it as written, and `get_definition` returns it so until an update gives another; an update that leaves it out keeps the overview saved. `list_definitions` leaves it out. [Reasoning functions](https://on.auto/docs/reference/http#reasoning-functions) gives the rules every definition follows, with `used_by`, the definitions of the playbook that use this one.
## Its page
A computation function's page is the `page` key of its front matter, written with the document and saved with it. It shows the person the figures the program worked out:
- `result`: the numbers, as figures or a table, such as the total spend in a `figure` chart and a row for each campaign in a table.
- `runs`: their series over time, such as the total spend of each period, keyed by the period the output names.

Show numbers over time as a chart keyed by the period a run is about, and anything else in its clearest form: a table, a list or a sentence. Show the value of the work, not telemetry: never how long the runtime took, a model's tokens or a run's id.

The fold sees the output alone, so give the output the period it is about, such as the month a run totals. The example's output names none, so its page keys each total by the day it was worked out: the spend so far, as of that day. Write amounts kept in cents as dollars, with `divided_by: 100` and `money`. [Page format](https://on.auto/docs/reference/page-format) says how to write `data`, `result` and `runs`.
## Availability
Computation functions are available in every runtime. See [Functions and availability](https://on.auto/docs/concepts/functions#availability).
# Generation function format

A generation function is a definition of the type `generation`. It produces an asset, an image or audio, from a prompt: its document names what it produces, a model of that kind, the parameters the model takes and a prompt template. A run renders the prompt from its input, asks the model through a model gateway, keeps the bytes the model made in the playbook, and answers with a reference to the asset. An image or audio is made while the run's call waits; a run of a generation the provider finishes later waits for it instead, as A generation the provider finishes later sets out.

Use one for the pictures and the spoken words a playbook makes. Writing text is a [reasoning function](https://on.auto/docs/reference/reasoning-format)'s work, and turning text into a file is a [computation function](https://on.auto/docs/reference/computation-format)'s.
## A function document
The source is Markdown: YAML front matter, then a Liquid prompt template. This example makes a picture of a product for its listing:
```markdown
description: A picture of the product for its listing
produces: image
model: gateway/openai/gpt-image-2
input:
schema:
type: object
required: [product]
properties:
product: { type: string }
parameters:
quality: high
expires: P30D
A studio photograph of {{ input.product }} on a white table, in soft daylight.
This one speaks a welcome:
```markdown
produces: audio
model: gateway/openai/gpt-4o-mini-tts
parameters:
voice: coral
format: mp3
Welcome to {{ input.shop }}. Today is {{ today }}.

To save it, call `create_definition` with `type: "generation"`, a function `name`, the document as `source`, and its `overview` and `diagram`. A save without a `diagram` is refused, so give the word `none` when a picture would add nothing; The overview says how to write both. To run it, call `run_definition` with the same type and name and its `input`. Both operations also need the playbook id, unless the MCP connection is scoped to that playbook.
A run answers the [asset](https://on.auto/docs/reference/output-shapes#asset) it made:
```json
"media_type": "image/png",
"address": "https://runtime.example.com/v1/orgs/acme/playbooks/shop/content/4977…?until=1793527200&sig=…",
## Fields
| Field | Required | Value |
| `description` | No | Text of 1 to 1,000 characters |
| `produces` | Yes | `image`, `audio` or `video`. The catalogue names no model that produces video, so a function that produces `video` is refused as it is saved; see The models |
| `model` | Yes | `gateway/model`: the name of a gateway of `MODEL_GATEWAYS`, then a model of the catalogue that produces that kind, such as `gateway/openai/gpt-image-2` |
| `input.schema` | No | A JSON Schema of the input. The input is a JSON object; one the schema does not allow is `invalid_input` |
| `parameters` | No | The parameters of the kind, each within the limits of the model |
| `references` | No | JSON Pointers into the input, such as `/photo`, each at the `id` of an asset of the playbook the model takes as a reference; see References |

| `expires` | No | How long the asset is kept, an ISO 8601 duration from one hour to 3,650 days, such as `P30D`. Without it, an asset is kept for the days the runtime keeps one, 90 unless its operator sets another |
| `page` | No | The [page](https://on.auto/docs/reference/page-format) that presents its runs |

The prompt is everything after the front matter. It is a [template](https://on.auto/docs/reference/template) that reads `input`, `today`, the date as `YYYY-MM-DD`, and `now`, the time in ISO 8601, and it must render text: a list or an object written whole is refused. For audio, the prompt is the text the model speaks.
### How a document is checked
These are refused when the definition is saved, each with its line and its pointer:
- a `produces` other than `image`, `audio` or `video`, and a `model` not written `gateway/model`;
- a model the catalogue does not name, with the models it names that produce that kind;
- a model the catalogue says was retired, naming the model to use instead;
- a model that produces another kind than `produces`;
- a parameter of another kind, and a parameter outside the limits of the model, naming the values it takes;
- more references than the model takes, or any for a model that takes none;
- an expiry that is no ISO 8601 duration or is outside its range;
- a prompt that does not parse, reads a property the input schema does not allow, or is missing.
A gateway the runtime is not given is not refused when the function is saved; its runs are.

Quote a text that holds ` #`, or a comma inside `{ }`, such as `description: 'Posts the notes in #deliveries'` or `{ note: 'Costs 1,000 a month' }`. Unquoted, YAML reads ` #` as the start of a comment and a comma there, even the one in `1,000`, as the start of another key, so the text ends early, and the save does not always say so.
## The models

The runtime keeps a catalogue of the models a generation function may name, each with the kind it produces and the limits of what it takes. A model is named as the gateway names it, after the gateway's own name: a gateway named `gateway` that serves `openai/gpt-image-2` is named `gateway/openai/gpt-image-2`. `list_generation_models` answers the catalogue a server holds, with the names of its gateways; see [Generation models](https://on.auto/docs/reference/mcp#generation-models).
| Model | Produces | Takes |

| `openai/gpt-image-2` | image | `size` `auto`, `1024x1024`, `1536x1024` or `1024x1536`; `quality` `auto`, `low`, `medium` or `high`; a prompt of up to 32,000 characters; up to 16 references of PNG, JPEG or WebP, each up to 50 MiB |
| `openai/gpt-image-2.6-flare` | image | The sizes, prompt and references of `openai/gpt-image-2`; `quality` `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max` or `auto` |
| `openai/tts-1` | audio | `voice` `alloy`, `echo`, `fable`, `onyx`, `nova` or `shimmer`; `format` `mp3`, `opus`, `aac`, `flac` or `wav`; a prompt of up to 4,096 characters |
| `openai/tts-1-hd` | audio | The same as `openai/tts-1` |

| `openai/gpt-4o-mini-tts` | audio | `voice` `alloy`, `ash`, `ballad`, `coral`, `echo`, `fable`, `nova`, `onyx`, `sage`, `shimmer` or `verse`; the formats of `openai/tts-1`; a prompt of up to 4,096 characters |

A gateway may not serve every model of the catalogue. A model it does not serve is answered by the gateway as not found when the function runs. The catalogue names no model that produces video, so a function that produces video is refused as it is saved.
### Parameters
| Kind | Parameter | Value |
| image | `size` | One of the sizes of the model, such as `1024x1024` |
| image | `aspect` | One of the aspects of the model, such as `16:9`, for a model that takes an aspect rather than a size |
| image | `quality` | One of the qualities of the model, such as `high`. Without it, the first quality the catalogue names for the model |
| audio | `voice` | One of the voices of the model. Without it, the first voice the catalogue names for the model |
| audio | `format` | One of the formats of the model: `mp3`, `opus`, `aac`, `flac` or `wav`. Without it, the first it names |
| audio | `duration` | A whole number of seconds within the model's, for a model that takes a duration |
| video | `size` | One of the sizes of the model, such as `1280x720`, which also sets its aspect |
| video | `duration` | A whole number of seconds within the model's. Without it, the fewest seconds the model makes |
A parameter the model has no values for is refused, such as an `aspect` for `openai/gpt-image-2`, and an `aspect` for any video, whose size sets it.
## References

A reference gives the model an asset of the playbook to work from, such as a photograph of a product to place in a new scene. `references` names where in the input each asset's `id` is, and the input holds the id an earlier run answered:
```markdown
produces: image
model: gateway/openai/gpt-image-2
references: [/photo]
The same product, {{ input.product }}, on a garden table.
A reference is never an address. Each one is checked as the run starts, and the run is `invalid_input` at its pointer, asking the model nothing, when:
- the input holds no text at the pointer;
- no asset of this playbook has that id, as for an asset of another playbook;
- the asset has expired;
- its media type is not one the model takes, or it is larger than the model takes of one reference;
- its content is no longer kept.
## The asset

A run keeps the bytes the model made as content of the playbook, at once, and records the asset on a stream of its own, `assets/{id}`, as the fact `asset_kept`. The fact holds the asset's media type, size and SHA-256, the kind, what made it as `made_by`, and when the asset expires, `expires_at`. For a generation function, `made_by.generation` holds the model, the prompt as rendered, the parameters sent, the references taken, each by its id and digest, the cost the gateway answered as `cost_usd` where it answered one, and `own_key`. Its context names the run and the definition that made it. An image a tool answers a reasoning function's run is an asset too, made by that call, `made_by.tool_call` ([The run's history](https://on.auto/docs/reference/reasoning-format#the-run-s-history)).
The reference a run answers is the [asset shape](https://on.auto/docs/reference/output-shapes#asset):
- `id` is the asset's id, which a later run takes as a reference;
- `media_type`, `bytes` and `sha256` describe its bytes. An image's media type is read from its bytes; audio's is the one the gateway answers, or that of its format;

- `address` is a [signed address](https://on.auto/docs/reference/http#content-at-a-signed-address) its bytes are read at without a key, which lasts 15 minutes, until `address_until`. Both are `null` where the runtime's own address is neither `https` nor a loopback address, since the runtime signs no address there. An address in the record of an earlier run has expired: `get_asset` reads the asset again by its `id`, with the model that made it, when it expires and an address signed as it is read, until the asset expires ([Generation functions](https://on.auto/docs/reference/http#generation-functions)).

When the asset expires, the runtime records `asset_expired` on the asset's stream, with its size, and its id as a reference is then refused. It then removes the content, unless another part of the playbook holds the same bytes, such as another asset made the same, or they were kept again within the last hour. Bytes another asset holds are removed when the last asset that holds them expires. Once the content is removed, the runtime records `asset_content_removed` on the asset's stream, with its size and digest, and an address answered before reads nothing more.
## How a run works
1. The input is checked against `input.schema`.
2. The prompt is rendered from the input, and checked against the most characters the model takes, each character a Unicode code point.
3. Each reference is read from the input and checked.
4. The playbook must have room left for assets.

5. The runtime asks the gateway once: `POST` to the gateway's `base_url` with `/images/generations` for an image, `/images/edits` with the references as files for an image with references, `/audio/speech` for audio, and `/videos` for a video, naming the seconds it asks for, with the gateway's key, headers and query parameters. For a generation the provider finishes later, the run then waits; see A generation the provider finishes later.

6. The asset is checked against the most bytes the runtime keeps of one asset of its kind as it is read. The playbook was checked against the most it keeps of all its assets before the gateway was asked, so two runs that finish together may take it past that by one asset.
7. The bytes are kept, the asset recorded, and its reference answered.
A run reaches outside the runtime, and a run asked again asks the gateway again and may cost again, so a workflow retries a generation function only where a second asset is wanted.
## A generation the provider finishes later
No model of the catalogue finishes later, since none produces video, so no run waits this way.

A model whose provider takes minutes to make what it is asked for, as a video's does, is waited for rather than answered within the run's call. The gateway answers the request with the id of what it is making, and the run stays `started`. Its record holds that id as `handle`, and when the run stops waiting as `waits_until`. A workflow's step that runs the function waits for it as a step waits for an answer to a request, and goes on with the asset once it is kept.

Meanwhile the runtime asks the gateway at `/videos/{id}` how the generation stands: five seconds after the request, then every 10, 20 and 30 seconds, or, where the provider says how far it has got, about half the time that leaves, from five seconds to a minute. Once the provider has made it, the runtime fetches its bytes from `/videos/{id}/content` and keeps them as an asset, as for an image, and the run succeeds with the asset's reference. Both are paths of the video API of a LiteLLM gateway.

A run waits 10 minutes at most, unless its operator sets another time from 1 to 60 minutes. A generation not made by then ends the run `unavailable`, kind `generation_timed_out`. One the provider fails to make ends the run as the gateway answers. Either way the run's record holds the cost the request spent. However many times the runtime finds a generation made, it keeps one asset of it, under an id the run's deferral gives.
## How a run ends
| Rejection | When |
| `invalid_input`, kind `input_schema` | The input is no JSON object, or the input schema does not allow it |
| `invalid_input` | The prompt cannot be rendered from the input, renders empty, or is longer than the model takes; or a reference cannot be used, at its pointer |
| `conflict`, kind `blocked_by_moderation` | The provider behind the gateway refused the request under its moderation. Change the prompt, the input or the references |
| `conflict`, kind `oversized` | The asset is larger than the runtime keeps of one asset of its kind, or the playbook already keeps all it may of its assets |
| `conflict`, kind `unworkable` | The gateway did not take the request, such as for a model it does not serve, or the catalogue no longer takes the model. Update the function |
| `unavailable`, kind `model_not_offered` | The model names a gateway the runtime is not given |

| `unavailable` | The gateway rejected its key, limited the rate, refused for its own budget or quota, answered a redirect, failed, did not answer within 240 seconds, or answered no image, no audio or no video; or the provider failed to make a generation it finishes later, or the gateway no longer knows it |
| `unavailable`, kind `generation_timed_out` | The provider had not made a generation it finishes later when the run had waited as long as it may. A new run asks for it again, which may cost again |

A run refused before the gateway answers keeps no asset and records no cost. A run the gateway answered and the runtime then refused, such as for an image larger than it keeps, or a generation it waited for in vain, keeps no asset and records the cost the gateway answered, since the model was asked.
## What a run records
A run that succeeds records the asset's reference as its output and, as its `record`:
| Field | Value |
| `model` | The model the document names |
| `own_key` | `true` where the gateway is reached with the key its entry of `MODEL_GATEWAYS` gives, the runtime operator's own, and `false` where the runtime reaches it with a key it is lent |
| `duration_ms` | How long the run took, for a generation the provider finishes later from the request to its bytes kept |
| `cost_usd` | The cost in US dollars the gateway answered in the header its entry names as `cost_header`, where it names one and answered a cost |

Each run counts once on the runtime's meter, as a run of every other function does. The meter counts the run, not the model call it makes. On hosted Auto, the model call uses credits of its own, in addition to the run's, as [Pricing](https://on.auto/pricing) explains.
## Bounds
| Bound | Default | Setting |
| One image | 20 MiB | `GENERATION_MAX_IMAGE_MIB`, from 1 to 1,024 |
| One asset of audio | 50 MiB | `GENERATION_MAX_AUDIO_MIB`, from 1 to 1,024 |
| One video | 200 MiB | `GENERATION_MAX_VIDEO_MIB`, from 1 to 4,096 |
| The assets of a playbook, together | 2,048 MiB | `GENERATION_MAX_PLAYBOOK_MIB` |
| How long an asset is kept without `expires` | 90 days | `GENERATION_RETENTION_DAYS`, from 1 to 3,650 |
| Waiting for a generation the provider finishes later | 10 minutes | `GENERATION_WAIT_MINUTES`, from 1 to 60 |
| The prompt | The model's | The catalogue |
| References | The model's | The catalogue |
| Waiting for the gateway | 240 seconds | |
| A run | 300 seconds | |
| A run of a generation the provider finishes later | The wait and 9 minutes more | `GENERATION_WAIT_MINUTES` sets the wait |

## Its page
A generation function's page is the `page` key of its front matter, written with the document and saved with it. It shows the person what the function made:

- `result`: the asset the run produced, said in the function's own words with its kind and size, such as `A picture of the product for its listing, 1.8 MB.`, and linked at its `address`. The run's output is the asset's reference, not the prompt it rendered, so `result` names what the function makes as its description does. The address lasts 15 minutes after the run, so the link opens the asset only until `address_until`, and a client shows an image as a link, never in the page.
